issues.title: `module.compile()` behaves differently from `torch.compile(module)`
issues.author: GdoongMathew
issues.body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

 `module.compile(backend=custom_backend)`'s forward method returns a different result from `torch.compile(module)`, especially when using `Conv2d`. 

## Example
```python
def print_fx_graph(graph: torch.fx.GraphModule, example_inputs: list[torch.Tensor]):
    print("Current graph:")
    graph.graph.print_tabular()
    return graph.forward


class Custom(torch.nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.module = torch.nn.Conv2d(3, 3, 3)

    def forward(self, x):
        return self.module(x)

if __name__ == "__main__":

    module = torch.nn.Conv2d(3, 3, 3)
    module.cuda().eval()
    image = torch.zeros((2, 3, 768, 768), device="cuda")

    torch._dynamo.reset()
    module.compile(backend=print_fx_graph)
    print(module(image).shape)

    torch._dynamo.reset()
    custom_module = Custom()
    custom_module.cuda().eval()
    custom_module.compile(backend=print_fx_graph)
    print(custom_module(image).shape)
```
>>>

issues.title: [nested compile region] silently incorrect result on global mutation
issues.author: zou3519
issues.body:
```
from dataclasses import dataclass

import torch


@dataclass
class RegionInput:
    hidden: torch.Tensor


region_input = RegionInput(torch.tensor(0))


@torch.compiler.nested_compile_region
def region():
    return region_input.hidden + 1


def fn(hidden):
    global region_input
    for _ in range(2):
        region_input = RegionInput(hidden)
        hidden = region()
    return hidden


hidden = torch.tensor(0)
expected = fn(hidden)
actual = torch.compile(fn, backend="eager", fullgraph=True)(hidden)

print(f"expected: {expected}")
print(f"actual:   {actual}")
torch.testing.assert_close(actual, expected)
```
gives
```
expected: 2
actual:   1
```

issues.title: AArch64 CPU - Inductor benchmark Regressions
issues.author: aditew01
issues.body: Regression noticed on upstream Compiler Inductor benchmarks after migration to OSDC (ARC) arm64 runners in this PR: https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/187994 (specifially with the Abs Execution Time field) The overall speedup from the benchmark suite is constant, it mighe be it sees similar slowdown in the Eager path. comments.body: @claude triage the issue

comments.author: claude[bot]
comments.body:
**Claude finished @aditew01's task in 2m 9s** —— [View job](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/actions/runs/28374551307)

---
### Issue Triage

- [x] Analyze the regression data and PR #187994 context
- [x] Investigate the runner migration (OSDC/ARC arm64)
- [x] Classify root cause & recommend labels/next steps

---

### Analysis

This is a **performance regression on AArch64 CPU** that appeared after migrating the Inductor benchmark jobs to the OSDC (ARC) arm64 runners in #187994. The comparison table shows large jumps in **Abs Execution Time** while accuracy stays `pass` and **Portable speedup stays roughly constant**, e.g.:

| Model | Abs exec time (pre → post) | Approx factor |
|---|---|---|
| `mobilenetv2_100` | 52.68ms → 158.30ms | ~3.0x |
| `deit_base_distilled_patch16_224` | 308.31ms → 514.01ms | ~1.7x |
| `mobilenetv3_large_100` | 309.20ms → 481.61ms | ~1.6x |
| `repvgg_a2` | 190.96ms → 292.04ms | ~1.5x |
| `ghostnet_100` | 138.14ms → 152.06ms | ~1.1x |

**Key signal:** the *speedup* (compiled vs. eager) is essentially unchanged, and you note eager regressed by a similar amount. That points away from a `torch.compile`/Inductor codegen regression and toward the **runner environment itself** — i.e. the new ARC arm64 hosts are measuring slower wall-clock than the previous runners. Common causes for this pattern after a runner migration:

- Different/older Neoverse core generation or lower sustained clocks (no turbo / power policy)
- Fewer vCPUs or different thread/affinity defaults (`OMP_NUM_THREADS`, core pinning, NUMA)
- Noisy-neighbor / shared-host contention or thermal throttling on the new fleet
- Different glibc / kernel / BLAS (e.g. OpenBLAS vs. Arm Compute Library) or `LD_PRELOAD` / allocator differences baked into the new image

Since absolute timings are not normalized across heterogeneous hardware, a runner migration legitimately shifts the baseline. The actionable question for whoever owns the benchmark fleet is whether the new ARC arm64 runners are spec-equivalent (CPU model, core count, threading env) to the pre-migration ones, and whether a fresh baseline needs to be captured for the dashboard.

### Suggested next diagnostics
- Compare `lscpu` / `nproc` / governor and the `OMP_NUM_THREADS` + thread-affinity settings between the old and new runner images.
- Confirm the same BLAS/ACL backend and version are present in both images.
- If the new fleet is intentionally different hardware, the benchmark dashboard baseline likely needs to be re-seeded post-migration rather than treated as a code regression.

### Recommended labels
Based on the [triage rubric](.claude/skills/triaging-issues), this is a CI-infrastructure-driven performance regression on ARM (root cause is the runner migration, not PT2 codegen), so:

- `module: arm`
- `module: ci`
- `module: performance`
- `module: regression`

> ⚠️ I was unable to apply these labels directly — the `mcp__github__issue_write` tooling isn't available in this session and the `gh` CLI requires an approval I don't have. A maintainer (cc @huydhn) can apply the labels above. If you'd like me to take any further action, please re-run with the appropriate `--allowedTools` granted.

issues.title: [inductor] `LoweringException: AssertionError` in `scatter_reduce_` lowering
issues.author: jasminetrail
issues.body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

## Summary
The `scatter_reduce_` lowering trips an assertion during compilation. Eager mode produces a valid tensor; only the `torch.compile(backend="inductor")` path fails. Ops involved: `AdaptiveMaxPool1d`, `scatter`.

## Repro
```python
# Minimal repro for crash 0fa013a0 (compiled-only: eager OK, inductor crashes)
import torch, torch.nn as nn, torch.nn.functional as F

_m_t7785 = torch.nn.AdaptiveMaxPool1d((0,), return_indices=False).eval()

torch.manual_seed(0)
t7782 = torch.rand([4, 8], dtype=torch.float32)

def model_828():
    t7784 = torch.special.ndtri(t7782)
    t7785 = _m_t7785(t7784)
    t7787 = torch.scatter(t7785, -1, t7785, t7785)
    t7788 = torch.nn.functional.hardswish(t7787, inplace=False)
    return t7788

# eager baseline -- succeeds
eager_out = model_828()
print("eager OK:", type(eager_out))

# inductor compile -- crashes
compiled = torch.compile(model_828, backend="inductor")
with torch.no_grad():
    compiled_out = compiled()
print("compiled OK:", type(compiled_out))
```
Eager runs successfully (`eager OK` prints); the crash happens in the compiled call.

issues.title: Dynamo runtime overhead in LLM Inference
issues.author: zou3519
issues.body: Setup: torch.compile on HF transformers qwen3-8b https://gist.github.com/zou3519/63fa2e77d7fcefe21c73d44e4e9190d6 ## the problem By default it looks like Dynamo cache lookup and pre-graph bytecode take ~2ms. This happens on every forward pass of the model: It's possible that this runtime overhead can matter depending on everything else the user does. The prefill in this profile is 41ms, which is a bit larger than 2ms, but a decode of this is probably going to be closer to 2ms than 41ms. Usually people use cudagraphs (on the outside of torch.compile) and/or make sure their gpu is fully utilized via other strategies, so it's plausible that the Dynamo CPU overhead can be hidden, but 2ms seems like a lot. We should try to bring down the 2ms as much as possible and/or document how to do it if we haven't already. ## some workarounds that bring the times down some noisy codex analysis: ``` Cumulative configuration Cache lookup Pregraph Combined overhead ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ ━━━━━━━━━━ ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ Baseline 0.761 ms 0.131 ms 0.892 ms ─────────────────────────────────────── ────────────── ────────── ─────────────────── + install_free_tensors=True 2.000 ms 0.006 ms 2.006 ms ─────────────────────────────────────── ────────────── ────────── ─────────────────── + skip_guard_eval_unsafe=True 0.105 ms 0.007 ms 0.112 ms ─────────────────────────────────────── ────────────── ────────── ─────────────────── + skip_guard_on_all_nn_modules_unsafe 0.038 ms 0.006 ms 0.044 ms ─────────────────────────────────────── ────────────── ────────── ─────────────────── + skip_all_guards_unsafe 0 ms 0.006 ms 0.006 ms ``` I'm surprised that skip_guard_eval_unsafe=True doesn't just skip all the guards, since I'm just compiling for one specialization. Unrelated but interesting: Inductor freezing mode is highly profitable because it combine the qkv weights all into one big buffer. codex tells me the forward pass latency goes from 20-26ms down to 10ms with freezing on. ## discussion cc @chauhang @penguinwu @voznesenskym @EikanWang @jgong5 @Guobing-Chen @XiaobingSuper @zhuhaozhe @blzheng @wenzhe-nrv @jiayisunx @kadeng @amjames @jataylo @azahed98 @anijain2305 @williamwen42

comments.author: zou3519
comments.body:
my codex says:
```
 Dynamo’s reuse cache cannot fingerprint the Hugging Face StaticCache argument. It appears as a UserDefinedObjectVariable, while reuse
 currently supports tensors, symbolic values, constants, and modules only.

 Consequently:

 1. Each layer fails is_reuse_eligible() at torch/_dynamo/variables/invoke_subgraph.py:425.
 2. Dynamo traces the layer again, costing roughly 120ms per layer.
 3. After tracing, graph comparison recognizes the resulting FX graphs as equivalent, so Inductor still compiles only one subgraph.

 A constant reuse key bypasses too much: Qwen’s self.layer_idx selects cache.layers[i]. Replaying layer 0’s cached trace therefore
 updates layer 0’s KV cache 36 times. We need reuse to parameterize the selected cache tensors, not merely declare every invocation
 identical.
```

issues.title: [RFC] Inductor / AOTI tests: decouple “correct codegen path” from tight eager-fp16 equality
issues.author: iupaikov-amd
issues.body:
## 1. Summary

- Many Inductor and AOTI tests **prove two things at once**: (a) the **compiled path** matches the scenario we care about, and (b) **eager fp16** matches **compiled fp16** to a very tight tolerance. Those goals are often unrelated.
- When eager/compiled check fails on one vendor or SKU while the logic path is fine, we get **noise in CI and review**: skips, tolerance PRs, and repeated explanation - without strengthening the signal for the original regression.
- **fp16** is usually a **red herring**: the interesting question is often **routing, grid, or reference choice**, not “bit-identical GEMM across every math backend.”
- **Dedicated suites already cover fp16 matmul accuracy** (OpInfo, matmul tests). Re-encoding the same bar in **narrow integration tests** duplicates work and **varies by architecture** (e.g. different reduction tiling across GPUs).
- **Ask:** treat this as an incremental cleanup opportunity — tests that were reasonable when written can be upgraded to match the failure mode (structure, reference dtype, or codegen hints) while staying **vendor-neutral**.

---

## 2. Example: `test_bmm_large_batch_dynamic` (AOTI BMM, large dynamic batch)

- PR [#178617](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/178617) introduced logic: **dynamic** batch BMM with **`B > 65535`** must **launch legally** and **index batches correctly** (Triton batch split across `grid_y` / `grid_z`). This logic is checked by comparing if eager vs compiled outputs are bitwise identical. While this in theory covers the regression, it also is prone to 1 ULP fp16 jitter due to reordering on different archs. 
- [#183630](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/183630) scaled inputs to reduce benign fp16 noise for CUDA, which is essentially a tolerance increase in disguise. This makes the test less flaky for **some** archs, but doesn't solve the root of the issue.
- Tight **`same()`** / eager-fp16 equality is **stricter than the bug** needs and **varies by hardware** (e.g. [#179958](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/179958), [#184531](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/184531)) — **false failures** even when the **grid fix** is sound.

---

## 3. Other examples (same pattern family)

| Link | Note |
|------|------|
| [#183630](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/183630) | `test_bmm_large_batch_dynamic` — input scaling / tolerance / CUDA follow-up |
| [#184531](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/184531) | `test_bmm_large_batch_dynamic` — tolerance / ROCm follow-up |
| [#182028](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/182028) | ROCm MI200 — flex vs SDPA `assert_close` tolerances |
| [#186889](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/186889) | XPU — relaxed `assertEqual` vs eager (atomic ordering) |
| [#169694](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/169694) | Transformer tests — **golden** precision / reference choice |
| [#183691](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/183691) | Test infra — tolerance overrides (helps **symptoms**; root cause is still design in individual tests) |

---

## 4. Conclusion & proposed next steps

- We would like to advocate for having some sort of test design guidelines to avoid such problems in the future and help to redesign some of the existing tests. Since this problem is universal for all vendors and multitude of archs we would like to bring this to your attention. As Inductor and hardware diversity grow, **narrowing the logic** per test is a good way to move forward.
- **Proposals (pick per test):**
  - **Match logic to risk:** grid / launch bugs → **shape, finiteness, boundary indices**, optional **codegen / log substring**; fp16 GEMM agreement → **leave to OpInfo / matmul** suites or use **FP32 reference + documented tol**.
  - **Tier or split checks:** small-shape **strict** + large-shape **reference-based**, so one failure mode doesn’t block the other.
  - **Document intent in-test** (one comment): what regression file / PR motivated the scenario—helps future edits stay aligned.
- **Proposed direction:** **FP32 matmul reference** (or similar), **boundary row checks** around **65535**, optional **Inductor log / codegen hints** for the batch reconstruction — **same regression intent**, **less coupling** to eager fp16 BLAS. I will link a draft PR to highlight what was described.

issues.title: [RFC][inductor] Support pre/post kernel execution hooks in compiled graphs
issues.author: yohaigevim
issues.body:
### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch

### Motivation

Inductor lowers an FX graph into a single Python wrapper (`call()`) that invokes
Triton and extern/fallback kernels in sequence. For tooling that needs to
observe the graph *as it actually runs* - not as it was traced - the wrapper is
the only place where the real kernel boundaries and the real tensor objects
(post-allocation, post-reuse, with concrete strides/data pointers) are visible.

Today there is no supported way to run user code at those boundaries. Tools that
need per-kernel runtime context are forced into bad options:

- **Patching generated code** - brittle, breaks on every codegen change, not
  portable across Inductor versions.
- **Whole-graph wrapping** - `torch.profiler` or wrapping `call()` gives one
  boundary for the entire graph, with no per-kernel name or tensor context.
- **Repurposing `generate_intermediate_hooks`** - that mechanism captures
  buffer *values* after a node for numerical debugging; it is not a callback
  around the kernel call and does not see inputs or extern kernels.

The concrete driver is **XPTI / Level-Zero profiling of Intel GPU workloads**:
to correlate each compiled kernel launch with external profiler events, we need
a callback at the kernel boundary that observes the kernel name and its
input/output tensors. The need is general, though - any per-kernel tracing or
analysis tool benefits: profiling correlation, tensor metadata capture
(dtype/shape/stride/device per boundary), or custom per-kernel
timers/counters/validation without forking codegen.

### Pitch

Add an **opt-in** config flag plus a context manager. When
`config.generate_node_hooks` is enabled, the generated wrapper emits a pre-hook
and a post-hook around each node:

```python
from torch._inductor.hooks import node_hook

def on_kernel(phase, kernel_name, tensors):
    # phase is "pre" or "post"
    ...

with node_hook(on_kernel):
    compiled_model(x)
```

### Design goals:

- **Zero overhead and zero codegen change when disabled** - the flag is `False`
  by default; with it off, not a single line of wrapper code differs.
- **Covers both Triton and extern/fallback kernels** - both are emitted into the
  wrapper, so both get hooks (verified for `mm` and pointwise fusions).
- **Real tensor objects, not metadata** - the callback receives the live tensors
  as the wrapper sees them, after allocation and inplace reuse.
- **Scoped and stackable** - hooks register via a context manager; multiple
  hooks compose.

The mechanism mirrors the existing `intermediate_hook` / `run_intermediate_hooks`
pair in `torch/_inductor/hooks.py`, but instruments the kernel call site rather
than buffer values.

| Symbol | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `config.generate_node_hooks` | Master opt-in flag (default `False`) |
| `node_hook(fn)` | Context manager to register a callback |
| `run_pre_node_hook` / `run_post_node_hook` | Emitted around each kernel in the wrapper |

Callback signature: `fn(phase: str, kernel_name: str, tensors: list[Tensor])`,
`phase ? {"pre", "post"}`.

### Alternatives

- **Extend `generate_intermediate_hooks`** - captures buffer *values* after a
  node for numerical debugging, not a callback around the kernel call; no
  inputs, no extern-kernel coverage. Overloading it would conflate two unrelated
  use cases and risk breaking existing users.
- **Wrap the compiled `call()` externally** - too coarse: one hook per whole
  graph, no per-kernel name/tensor context.
- **`torch.profiler`** - gives timing, but no user callback with access to the
  kernel name and input/output tensors at the Inductor node level.

### Open questions for maintainers

- **Callback signature.** Is `(phase, name, tensors)` the right shape, or would
  separate pre/post callbacks (mirroring forward/backward hooks elsewhere in
  PyTorch) be preferred? Should the node/IR handle be passed alongside the
  tensors?
- **Scope of coverage.** Hooks only cover work emitted into the wrapper. Graph
  breaks and `torch._dynamo.disable` regions run outside it and won't fire;
  extern/fallback ops *inside* the wrapper are covered. Is documenting this
  limitation sufficient, or is broader coverage expected?

### Additional context

**Scope is by design, not a gap.** The purpose is to instrument the *compiled*
graph, where no per-kernel callback exists today. Eager execution already has
well-established ways to instrument kernels - `TorchDispatchMode` /
`__torch_dispatch__`, `torch.library` op registration/wrapping, and
`torch.profiler` - so this proposal fills the compiled-path gap, not the eager
one.

A working implementation with tests exists and is ready to send as a PR once
this is marked actionable:
https://github.com/yohaigevim/pytorch/tree/node-hooks

comments.author: EikanWang
comments.body: @yohaigevim have you tried unitrace?

comments.author: yohaigevim
comments.body:
Hi @EikanWang, thanks for the pointer.

Yes. Our team actually works on unitrace, and the tooling we're building sits on top of the same L0/XPTI interception layer, so the low-level tracing side is covered.

The gap is different: mapping intercepted L0 kernel launches back to the Inductor node that produced them. By the time a launch hits the driver, the FX/Inductor structure (node name, per-node input/output tensors) is gone, and reconstructing it from kernel names or launch order is brittle.

A small hook on the wrapper side, firing right before/after each node's kernel call with access to its inputs/outputs, lets us emit one XPTI marker per node and correlate cleanly on the C++ side.

comments.author: EikanWang
comments.body: @yohaigevim , the pain points described in this RFC are across different hardware backends but not XPU specific, right?

comments.author: yohaigevim
comments.body:
> [@yohaigevim](https://github.com/yohaigevim) , the pain points described in this RFC are across different hardware backends but not XPU specific, right?

  Hi @EikanWang , correct - it's backend-agnostic.

  The hook fires in the Inductor wrapper (call()), which is shared codegen, not device-specific. It wraps each node's kernel
  call regardless of where the kernel runs, so the same flag works for CUDA, XPU, CPU, or any backend, and there is no XPU- or
  L0-specific code in the mechanism itself.

  XPTI/Level-Zero is just our concrete driving use case (the first consumer), not the boundary of the feature. Any tool that
  needs per-kernel runtime context at the compiled-graph level benefits equally:

  - profiler correlation - map a launch back to its Inductor node on any backend
  - tensor metadata capture - real dtype/shape/stride/device per kernel boundary
  - per-kernel timers, counters, or numerical validation without forking codegen

  The only thing that is inherently device-agnostic and only exists in the compiled path is the node boundary itself, which is
  precisely what this exposes.

issues.title: cumsum appears non-deterministic under torch.compile even when use_deterministic_algorithms is enabled
issues.author: christopherhesse
issues.body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

cumsum appears non-deterministic under torch.compile even when use_deterministic_algorithms is enabled

```python
import torch


NUMEL = 1_000_003
REPEATS = 10


def check_repeats(name, fn, x):
    reference = fn(x)
    torch.cuda.synchronize()

    mismatches = 0
    first_mismatch = None
    max_abs_diff = 0.0
    for _ in range(REPEATS):
        result = fn(x)
        torch.cuda.synchronize()
        different = reference.view(torch.int32) != result.view(torch.int32)
        if different.any():
            mismatches += 1
            index = int(torch.where(different)[0][0])
            first_mismatch = (
                index if first_mismatch is None else min(first_mismatch, index)
            )
            max_abs_diff = max(
                max_abs_diff, float((reference - result).abs().max())
            )

    print(
        f"{name}: mismatches={mismatches}/{REPEATS}, "
        f"first_mismatch={first_mismatch}, max_abs_diff={max_abs_diff}"
    )


if not torch.cuda.is_available():
    raise RuntimeError("This reproduction requires a CUDA GPU")

print(f"torch={torch.__version__}")
print(f"cuda={torch.version.cuda}")
print(f"gpu={torch.cuda.get_device_name(0)}")

docs = torch.use_deterministic_algorithms.__doc__ or ""
print(
    "docs_list_float_cuda_cumsum_as_unsupported="
    f"{'cumsum' in docs and 'floating point or complex' in docs}"
)

torch.manual_seed(0)
torch.use_deterministic_algorithms(True, warn_only=False)
x = torch.randn(NUMEL, device="cuda", dtype=torch.float32)

check_repeats("eager", lambda value: torch.cumsum(value, dim=0), x)

compiled_cumsum = torch.compile(lambda value: torch.cumsum(value, dim=0))
check_repeats("compiled", compiled_cumsum, x)
```

```
eager: mismatches=0/10, first_mismatch=None, max_abs_diff=0.0
compiled: mismatches=10/10, first_mismatch=6144, max_abs_diff=0.001220703125
```

issues.title: [Inductor][CPU] torch.compile returns 0 for short positive uint8/int8 amin reductions on Apple Silicon
issues.author: lackjava-creator
issues.body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

On an Apple Silicon CPU, Inductor returns `0` for a short positive `uint8` or `int8` `amin` reduction, while eager execution returns the correct minimum. This is a silent wrong-result issue and reproduces on the first compiled call with a fresh Inductor cache.

The problem occurs with both static and dynamic compilation. A four-element tensor is sufficient; lengths 1–3 pass in my local checks, while lengths 4 and above fail.

### Minimal reproducer

```python
import torch

print("torch:", torch.__version__)
print("git:", torch.version.git_version)

for dtype in (torch.uint8, torch.int8):
    x = torch.tensor([5, 6, 7, 8], dtype=dtype)

    for dynamic in (False, True):
        torch._dynamo.reset()
        compiled_fn = torch.compile(
            lambda value: torch.amin(value),
            backend="inductor",
            fullgraph=True,
            dynamic=dynamic,
        )

        eager = torch.amin(x)
        compiled = compiled_fn(x)
        print(dtype, "dynamic=", dynamic,
              "eager=", eager.item(),
              "compiled=", compiled.item())

        torch.testing.assert_close(compiled, eager, rtol=0, atol=0)
```

Observed on PyTorch 2.13.0:

```text
torch.uint8 dynamic=False eager=5 compiled=0
torch.uint8 dynamic=True  eager=5 compiled=0
torch.int8  dynamic=False eager=5 compiled=0
torch.int8  dynamic=True  eager=5 compiled=0
```

Expected: all compiled results are `5`.

### Isolation results

- Reproduced 3/3 with a new `TORCHINDUCTOR_CACHE_DIR` each time.
- `uint8` and `int8` fail; `int16`, `int32`, `int64`, `float16`, and `float32` pass for the same values.
- Setting `torch._inductor.config.cpp.simdlen = 1` makes the `uint8` and `int8` cases correct.
- PyTorch 2.5.1 on the same machine returns the correct result for this reproducer.

The failing generated C++ uses a partial vector load followed by an unmasked vector minimum and horizontal minimum, approximately:

```cpp
auto tmp0 = at::vec::Vectorized<uint8_t>::loadu(in_ptr0, 4);
tmp_acc0_vec = at::vec::minimum(tmp_acc0_vec, tmp0);
tmp_acc0 = at::vec::vec_reduce_all<uint8_t, 1>(
    [](auto& x, auto& y) { return at::vec::minimum(x, y); },
    tmp_acc0_vec);
```

A possible explanation is that inactive lanes from the partial vector load participate as zero in the horizontal minimum. This is only a code-generation hint; the reproducer and `simdlen=1` control are the confirmed observations.

### Environment

```text
PyTorch: 2.13.0
PyTorch git: cf30153c4c131c8164ee7798e5022d810682e2cb
Python: 3.12.10
OS: macOS 26.0 arm64
Machine: Apple M1 Pro / arm64
Backend: Inductor CPU
```

issues.author: xyt66665000

comments.author: xyt66665000
comments.body:
I took a quick look, and this seems related to the new prims.uniform decomposition from #187887.

It looks like the compiled path does not handle sliced, non-contiguous views correctly, which can lead to reading invalid memory and returning garbage values. Eager mode takes a different path and works as expected.

I do not have time to work on a fix right now, so feel free to pick this up and send a PR.
